title: The Concept of the Mixing Index
content:
Abstract

Many current measures of mixing, such as the statistics of concentration, the scalar dissipation rate, or dilution index, are based on the dilution of a single component or pseudo-component. Because of this, they miss the influence of numerous conditions that directly change true mixing, such as initial separation of chemically distinct water bodies. Two measures of the overlap of density functions—the Kullback/Leibler and Jensen/Shannon cross-entropies—naturally account for separation of dissolved plumes, and lead to a mixing index that varies between zero (completely unmixed) and unity (perfectly mixed). The mixing index and its time derivative (the mixing rate) can be solved exactly for simple plume geometries, and show the dependence on multi-plume conditions including initial separation or disparate transport properties. The Jensen/Shannon version is better suited to hydrology because of the way zero concentrations are handled. When applied to a variety of examples, we find that the conceptualization of local dispersion and mixing has a large effect on the observed mixing rates. The complex interplay of initial conditions, nonuniform and nonsteady velocity and anisotropic, velocity-dependent dispersion has a great effect on overall mixing rates, implying that a full dispersion tensor is needed to quantify mixing in complex and unsteady flows above the pore scale. We also show that the new Jensen/Shannon mixing index and rate can be applied to any number of solute plumes and reactive solutes.
